title: Still Drunk the Next Morning? How to Tell and How Long It Lasts
excerpt: Can you still be drunk the next morning? How to tell leftover intoxication from a hangover, why sleep may not be enough, why coffee won't help, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you still be drunk the next morning? How to tell drunk from hungover, why sleep may not sober you up, why not to drive, and alcohol poisoning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, you can absolutely still be drunk the next morning. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for most people, and nothing you do speeds that up much. If your blood alcohol was high when you went to bed, a few hours of sleep may not be enough to bring it back to zero. Many people who feel "just hungover" at 7 a.m. are actually still over the legal driving limit.

**The quick rules:** If you drank heavily until late, assume you are still impaired the next morning until enough time has passed. Don't drive, don't operate machinery, and don't make big decisions until you're sure. Coffee, cold showers, and greasy breakfasts make you feel more alert, but they do not lower your blood alcohol.

> **When to get medical help now.** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone **can't be woken up**, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths), has blue or pale, cold skin, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and they can show up the next morning, not just at the party. Don't leave them to "sleep it off." Also get help if you are confused, can't stop vomiting, or can't keep water down for many hours. If you drink heavily every day and wake up shaking, sweating, very anxious, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor the same day. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Can You Still Be Drunk the Next Morning?

Yes, and it happens more often than people think. Being drunk is not a feeling. It's a level of alcohol in your blood, usually measured as blood alcohol concentration (BAC). Your BAC goes up while you drink and for a while after, then comes down only as fast as your liver can process the alcohol.

That pace is the key. The liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly steady rate. For an average adult, BAC drops by somewhere around 0.015 percentage points per hour, and most people fall somewhere between about 0.010 and 0.020 per hour. That is a slow, steady trickle, not a drain you can unplug.

Now picture a typical big night. Someone drinks from 9 p.m. to 1 a.m., reaches a BAC near 0.15 to 0.20, and falls asleep at 2 a.m. By 8 a.m., seven hours after that last drink, they've cleared roughly 0.10. That leaves them somewhere around 0.05 to 0.10. In the US, the legal limit for driving is 0.08 for most adults (0.05 in Utah, 0.04 for commercial drivers, and effectively zero for drivers under 21). So the person who "slept it off" might still be over the limit when they get in the car to grab breakfast.

Sleep doesn't speed this up. Your liver works at the same pace whether you're asleep, awake, or jogging around the block. Sleep only passes the time.

## Still Drunk or Hungover? How to Tell the Difference

This is the question most people are really asking. The two can feel similar, and they can overlap. A hangover usually starts as your BAC is falling toward zero, so it's common to be a little of both at once in the early morning.

Here are the clues that point toward **still drunk**:

- **You feel oddly fine, or even a bit buzzed or giddy.** Many people mistake leftover intoxication for "not being hungover yet." The headache and nausea often arrive later, once the alcohol is mostly gone.
- **Your balance and coordination are off.** You bump into door frames, stumble on stairs, or fumble with your phone.
- **Your speech or thinking is slow.** Words come out slurred, or you lose track of what you were saying.
- **You can smell alcohol on your own breath strongly, or someone else can.** Breath odor isn't a reliable measure, but a strong, fresh alcohol smell suggests there's still plenty being exhaled.
- **You went to bed only a few hours ago after heavy drinking.** Timing is the most reliable clue of all.
- **Your judgment feels a bit loose.** Ideas that would normally seem bad (driving, texting your ex, an early swim) seem fine.

Here are the clues that point toward **mostly hungover**:

- **Pounding headache, thirst, and a dry mouth.** These tend to peak as BAC returns to zero.
- **Nausea or an upset stomach.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and the effect lingers after the alcohol leaves.
- **Sensitivity to light and sound.**
- **Fatigue, shakiness, and low mood or anxiety.** Poor sleep and the body's rebound after alcohol drive much of this.
- **Many hours have passed.** If you stopped drinking 12 or more hours ago after a moderate night, you are probably at or near zero.

The tricky truth: feeling terrible doesn't mean you're sober, and feeling fine doesn't mean you're sober either. Hangover symptoms and leftover alcohol both slow your reaction time. Research on next-day performance has found that people with a hangover can show impairment on driving and attention tasks even after their BAC is back to zero, which we cover in our guide to [driving hungover](/never-hungover/driving-hungover).

For a full list of hangover symptoms and what each one means, see our [hangover symptoms guide](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms).

## Why You Can't Work Out Your Own Morning BAC

There is no reliable way to work out at home whether you're sober enough to drive, and this page won't give you a formula for it. Online calculators and rules of thumb are built on averages, and the errors run in the dangerous direction: they assume you counted every drink correctly, that your pours were standard size, and that your liver works at an average pace.

In real life, all three are usually off. A US standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol, roughly 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. A strong IPA can count as nearly two drinks, a generous wine pour as one and a half, and a cocktail with two shots as two. Most people undercount, especially late in the night. Body size, sex, food, medicines, liver health, and how fast you drank all change how high your BAC got and how quickly it falls, and smaller people, women, and anyone who drank fast are often slower than the averages suggest.

So treat any estimate as a reason for caution, never as permission. If you had a heavy night, the safe assumption is that you may still be impaired, and the safe plan is not to drive at all that morning. Our explainer on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) covers how blood alcohol is measured, and our guide to [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains why the timing varies so much from person to person.

The pattern to watch for: the danger zone is a heavy night that ends late, followed by an early start.

## Why Alcohol Lingers: What Your Body Is Actually Doing

Understanding the mechanics helps explain why there's no shortcut.

**Absorption keeps going after your last drink.** Alcohol is absorbed mostly from your small intestine. If you drank a lot in the last hour or two of the night, some of that alcohol is still being absorbed when you go to bed. Your BAC can keep rising for 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, sometimes longer after a big final round. This is also why people can become dangerously drunk after they've passed out.

**The liver works at a steady pace.** The main enzyme that breaks down alcohol, alcohol dehydrogenase, gets saturated at fairly low levels of alcohol. Once it's working at full capacity, it can't go faster just because there's more alcohol waiting. That's why elimination is roughly linear: about the same amount each hour, no matter how much is in your blood.

**The by-product sticks around too.** Alcohol is turned into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that contributes to nausea, flushing, and the general misery of the next day. Your body then converts acetaldehyde to acetate, which is far less harmful. How fast this happens depends partly on your genes.

**Your own body changes the speed.** Things that tend to make morning BAC higher or slower to fall include:

- Smaller body size
- Being female (on average, less body water for the same weight)
- Drinking fast or on an empty stomach (higher peak)
- Liver disease or certain medications
- Older age
- Not being a regular drinker (people who drink heavily often can clear alcohol a bit faster, which is not a good sign for their health in other ways)

For a deeper dive on timing, see [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) and [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up).

## Can You Sober Up Faster in the Morning? Myths vs Reality

People try everything. Here's what each trick actually does.

| Trick | Does it lower your BAC? | What it actually does |
|---|---|---|
| Coffee | No | Makes you feel more awake. You become a wide-awake drunk person, which can be riskier because you feel more capable than you are. |
| Cold shower | No | A jolt of alertness. No effect on the alcohol in your blood. |
| Big breakfast | No, not once alcohol is absorbed | Food eaten **before or while** drinking slows absorption and lowers your peak. Food the next morning helps your stomach and blood sugar but doesn't remove alcohol already in your blood. |
| Drinking lots of water | No | Helps with thirst and dehydration symptoms. It doesn't flush out alcohol meaningfully, since only a tiny share leaves through urine. |
| Exercise or sweating | No, not meaningfully | Very little alcohol leaves through sweat and breath. Hard exercise while still intoxicated raises the risk of falls and injury. |
| Throwing up | Only if you drank very recently | Can remove alcohol still in the stomach right after drinking, but by morning the alcohol is in your blood. Vomiting just dehydrates you further. |
| Electrolyte drinks | No | Can help you feel better if you're dehydrated. No effect on BAC. |
| Going back to sleep | No, but time passes | The only thing that works is time. Sleeping is a fine way to spend it, as long as you're not dangerously intoxicated. |

The bottom line: **time is the only thing that lowers your BAC.** Everything else just changes how you feel while you wait. Our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) goes through the evidence in more detail.

## Is It Safe to Drive the Morning After Drinking?

Often, no. This is the most important practical point in this whole article.

Police in several countries, including the UK, run "morning after" awareness campaigns because a meaningful share of drink-driving arrests happen the next morning, often from people who honestly believed they were fine after sleeping. The legal limit is based on your BAC, not on how you feel or how long you slept.

A sensible approach:

- **If you had a heavy night that ended late, don't plan to drive early.** Book a later start, arrange a ride, or take public transit.
- **When in doubt, don't drive.** No rule of thumb, app, or breathalyzer can tell you you're safe after a heavy night.
- **Remember the hangover itself impairs you.** Even at zero BAC, a bad hangover slows reaction time and attention.
- **Lower limits apply to some drivers.** Commercial drivers in the US have a 0.04 limit, and drivers under 21 face zero-tolerance laws. Many countries outside the US use 0.05 or lower.

Personal breathalyzers can give you a rough idea, but consumer devices vary in accuracy and can read low. Treat a "safe" reading with suspicion if the timing says otherwise, and never use one to justify driving when you're unsure. Read more in [how long after drinking can you drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive).

## Still Drunk at Work or School

If you wake up and realize you're still intoxicated with a shift or class ahead, a few practical points:

- **Don't drive there.** Get a ride or take transit, or arrange to start later.
- **Be honest about safety-sensitive work.** If your job involves driving, machinery, ladders, medical care, childcare, or anything where a mistake could hurt someone, you should not be doing it while impaired. Calling in or swapping a shift is the responsible choice.
- **Workplace alcohol tests measure BAC.** Some employers and industries test, and a positive result from the night before counts just the same.
- **Eat, hydrate, and give it time.** You'll feel better, though your BAC will drop at its own pace.

## Alcohol Poisoning the Next Day: Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

> **Alcohol poisoning isn't only a party-night problem.** Because absorption continues after the last drink, someone who went to sleep very drunk can be in more danger a few hours later than when they lay down. Check on them. Call 911 right away if you see any of these:
>
> - They can't be woken up, or wake briefly and drift off again
> - Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or long pauses between breaths
> - Blue-tinged, gray, or very pale skin, or lips that look blue
> - Low body temperature, cold and clammy skin
> - Seizures
> - Vomiting while not fully awake (risk of choking)
> - Confusion or stupor that isn't improving
>
> While you wait for help: don't leave them alone, roll them onto their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower. In the US you can also call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for advice. More detail is in our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs).

It helps to know that people who get help for a friend are doing the right thing. Many US states and colleges have medical amnesty or Good Samaritan policies designed so that people aren't afraid to call for help in an alcohol emergency.

## When to See a Doctor (Not an Emergency, but Don't Ignore It)

Most "still drunk" mornings resolve with time, food, water, and rest. But check in with a doctor or urgent care if:

- You keep vomiting and can't keep fluids down for more than several hours, especially if you're dizzy when you stand or barely urinating
- You hit your head the night before, even if you felt fine at the time
- You have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or severe stomach pain
- You can't remember large parts of the night (a blackout) and are worried about what happened
- You took medication with alcohol, especially sleep aids, opioids, anxiety medicines, or anything with acetaminophen in it

**A note on withdrawal.** If you've been drinking heavily most days for weeks or longer, waking up with shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, strong anxiety, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become dangerous, including seizures, so don't try to tough it out or treat it with another drink. Talk to a doctor the same day, or go to urgent care. Our article on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the difference between normal next-day shakiness and warning signs.

## How to Avoid Waking Up Still Drunk

The fix isn't a morning trick. It happens the night before.

- **Set a stop time.** If you need to be up and functional at 8 a.m., your last drink should be many hours before bed. A useful planning habit: count back one hour per drink from when you need to be sober, and add a buffer.
- **Eat a real meal before you start.** Food in your stomach slows absorption and lowers your peak BAC, which means less to clear overnight.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour, and alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.
- **Watch drink strength.** Strong beers, big wine pours, and mixed drinks with multiple shots add up faster than you think.
- **Skip the "last round."** The final drinks of the night are the ones still being absorbed while you sleep.
- **Plan transport the night before.** Decide how you're getting home and how you're getting anywhere the next morning, before you start drinking.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the rest of the next-day picture.

## What About DHM and Other Supplements?

You may see supplements marketed as ways to "sober up" or "beat" a hangover. Be careful with those claims. **No supplement can make you sober faster in any way that matters for driving or safety.** Your BAC still falls at your liver's pace.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that some people take before or while drinking to help with how they feel the next day. Animal research suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it has been studied for its effects on the brain's GABA receptors in rats. Human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol enough to make driving or working safe. If you want to try it for next-day comfort, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). See our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for how people use it. Either way, the rules above still apply: count your drinks, give it time, and don't drive until you're sure.

## The Bottom Line

- You can easily still be drunk the next morning after a heavy night that ended late. Sleep passes the time but doesn't speed up your liver.
- Your BAC drops by roughly 0.015 per hour on average, about one standard drink per hour, and slower for many people.
- Feeling fine is not proof you're sober. Leftover intoxication often feels like "not hungover yet."
- Coffee, cold showers, breakfast, water, and exercise don't lower your BAC. Only time does.
- Don't drive or do safety-sensitive work until enough time has passed.
- Someone who can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or has blue or cold skin needs 911, even the next morning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you still be drunk the next morning?**

Yes. Your liver clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, or about 0.015 BAC per hour on average. If you drank heavily until late, a few hours of sleep may not be enough to bring you back to zero, and you could still be over the legal driving limit in the morning.

**How do I know if I'm still drunk or just hungover?**

Clues that you're still drunk include feeling oddly fine or buzzed, poor balance, slurred speech, loose judgment, and having gone to bed only a few hours after heavy drinking. Hangover symptoms like headache, thirst, and nausea usually peak as your BAC reaches zero. Timing matters too: if you drank heavily and slept only a few hours, assume you may still be impaired.

**How long does it take to stop being drunk?**

It depends on how much you drank and how fast your body clears alcohol. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, but that pace varies a lot between people, and after a heavy night it can take well into the next day. No home estimate is reliable enough to decide whether you can drive, so if you drank heavily, plan not to drive that morning at all.

**Is it safe to drive the morning after drinking?**

Often not after a heavy night. Many people are still over the legal limit the next morning without realizing it, and the hangover itself slows reaction time. If you drank heavily and slept only a few hours, arrange another way to travel or start later.

**Does coffee or a cold shower sober you up?**

No. They make you feel more alert but do nothing to the alcohol in your blood. Feeling more awake while still intoxicated can actually be riskier, because you may think you're fine to drive when you aren't.

**Can your blood alcohol keep rising while you sleep?**

Yes, for a while. Alcohol from the last drinks of the night is still being absorbed, so BAC can keep rising for 30 to 90 minutes or more after your last drink. This is why someone who passes out very drunk needs to be watched, placed on their side, and not left alone if they show signs of alcohol poisoning.

**What are signs of alcohol poisoning the next morning?**

Being unable to wake up, slow or irregular breathing, blue or pale and cold skin, seizures, vomiting while barely conscious, and confusion that isn't improving. Call 911 right away. Don't let them sleep it off.

**Can a supplement like DHM sober you up faster?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement lowers your blood alcohol enough to make driving or working safe. Some people use DHM for how they feel the next day, but time is the only thing that brings your BAC down.
